Title: Forecasting weekly demand for fresh produce in a small grocery chain

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A regional grocery chain with nine stores throws away about one tenth of its fresh produce each week because orders are placed from a simple moving average. Store managers and the chain's buyers are affected, through lost margin and empty shelves.
Research question. Can gradient boosting forecast weekly demand for fresh produce more accurately than the chain's current moving-average method?
Objectives.
1. Build a baseline moving-average forecast for ten produce items.
2. Train and tune a gradient boosting model on two years of sales.
3. Test whether weather variables improve accuracy.
Expected contribution. The work gives the chain a tested forecasting approach it can adopt, and adds evidence on whether weather data is worth collecting for small retailers.
Pathway. Predictive Modelling

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A comparative model study using historical sales split by time.
Data. Weekly sales for ten produce items across nine stores from January 2024 to June 2026 (about 4,000 rows), provided under a written access agreement signed on 18 September 2026, plus public weather records from the national weather service.
Method. A moving-average baseline, gradient boosting with time-series cross-validation (objectives 1 and 2), and the same model with weather variables added (objective 3).
Evaluation. I will compare mean absolute percentage error against the chain's current moving-average forecast on a held-out final eight weeks.
Feasibility. The main risk is missing sales weeks caused by store system outages. I will fill gaps with the previous year's value and report how many were filled.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Model building and tuning: December 2026 to January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Weather experiment and write-up: March to April 2027
M4 Final submission: 14 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Retail forecasting studies mostly use large supermarkets and daily data (Adler, 2019; Bianchi, 2020). Few test small chains with short sales histories, and weather is rarely compared on equal terms (Costa, 2021). My project responds to this gap.

References
Adler, A. (2019) Demand forecasting for perishable goods. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
Bianchi, B. (2020) Gradient boosting in grocery sales. International Journal of Forecasting Studies, 8(1).
Costa, C. (2021) Weather and retail demand: a review. Proceedings of the Business Data Conference.
Dumont, D. (2022) Moving averages in practice. Decision Analytics Review, 15(2).
Eriksen, E. (2023) Spoilage in fresh supply chains. Journal of Operations Research Practice, 9(4).

Title: Reducing order picking time in a mid-sized distribution warehouse

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. Pickers at a mid-sized distribution warehouse walk long, uneven routes, and customers wait longer for orders at peak times. Warehouse staff and customers are both affected.
Research question. Which changes to the slotting of fast-moving items would shorten average picking time per order the most?
Objectives.
1. Map the current picking routes from scanner logs.
2. Simulate three alternative slotting layouts.
3. Compare the layouts on time per order.
4. Estimate the saving in picker hours per week.
Expected contribution. A reusable simulation approach and a ranked list of layout changes for the warehouse.
Pathway. Process and Operations Analytics

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A simulation study built on observed picking logs.
Data. I will use the public order-picking benchmark dataset released by the Open Logistics Archive, which contains 120,000 pick lines and needs no permission.
Method. Route mapping (objective 1), discrete-event simulation (objectives 2 and 4) and a comparison of layouts with paired tests (objective 3).
Evaluation. I will judge whether the results look sensible and useful to the warehouse.
Feasibility. The main risk is that the simulation takes longer than planned, so I will build the simplest layout first and add detail only if time allows.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Route mapping and simulation set-up: December 2026 to January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Layout experiments and write-up: March to April 2027
M4 Final submission: 14 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Studies of order picking focus on routing algorithms (Adler, 2019; Dumont, 2022) and assume the layout is fixed. Few test slotting changes against real scanner logs, so my project addresses that gap.

References
Adler, A. (2019) Order picking: a survey. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
Bianchi, B. (2020) Slotting in distribution centres. International Journal of Forecasting Studies, 8(1).
Costa, C. (2021) Simulation of warehouse operations. Proceedings of the Business Data Conference.
Dumont, D. (2022) Walking distance in manual picking. Decision Analytics Review, 15(2).
Eriksen, E. (2023) Picker productivity and layout. Journal of Operations Research Practice, 9(4).
Farouk, F. (2019) Discrete-event simulation for logistics. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
Grant, G. (2020) Warehouse layout guide. Practitioner guide.
Hale, H. (2021) Peak-season staffing note. Web page, accessed 2026.

Title: Why subscribers cancel a meal-kit service: a survey-based churn study

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A meal-kit subscription company loses about a third of new subscribers within three months. Its marketing and product teams do not know whether price, variety or delivery problems drive cancellations, so retention offers are guesses.
Research question. Which reasons for cancelling are most common among subscribers who leave within three months?
Objectives.
1. Survey recent former subscribers about their reasons for leaving.
2. Group the reasons into themes and rank them.
3. Compare the themes between price-driven and delivery-driven leavers.
Expected contribution. The company gets an evidence-based list of churn reasons, and the study adds a small data point on early churn in subscription food services.
Pathway. Customer and Market Analytics

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A cross-sectional online survey with a short follow-up interview.
Data. A survey of 150 former subscribers, recruited by e-mail through the company's mailing list under a written access agreement dated 25 September 2026.
Method. Thematic coding of open answers (objective 2) and a chi-square test of theme frequencies between groups (objective 3).
Evaluation. Success means at least 100 completed surveys and a top-ranked theme that differs from the second theme at the 5 percent significance level.
Feasibility. The main risk is a low response rate, so I will send two reminders and offer a small prize draw.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Ethics application submitted: 1 December 2026
Survey fieldwork: January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Coding and analysis: March 2027
Writing up: April 2027
M4 Final submission: 14 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Churn research in subscriptions is dominated by model-based studies built on usage logs, as shown in earlier work [2], [3]. Few studies ask leavers directly why they left, which limits what retention teams can act on. My project responds to this gap.

References
Adler, A. (2019) Churn in subscription services. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
Bianchi, B. (2020) Why customers cancel. International Journal of Forecasting Studies, 8(1).
Costa, C. (2021) Retention offers and price. Proceedings of the Business Data Conference.
Dumont, D. (2022) Survey methods for leavers. Decision Analytics Review, 15(2).
Eriksen, E. (2023) Thematic coding in practice. Journal of Operations Research Practice, 9(4).
Farouk, F. (2019) Meal-kit market trends. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
Grant, G. (2020) Subscription economy overview. Practitioner guide.
Hale, H. (2021) Delivery quality and loyalty. Web page, accessed 2026.

Title: A waste-tracking dashboard for a regional bakery chain

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A bakery chain with twelve shops records unsold bread on paper sheets, and head office sees the figures only at month end. Shop managers and the operations director cannot react to waste in time.
Research question. Which waste indicators, shown in a weekly dashboard, help shop managers cut unsold bread?
Objectives.
1. Define five waste indicators with the operations director.
2. Build a dashboard prototype that updates weekly.
3. A usability test with six shop managers.
Expected contribution. Shop managers get a tested weekly view of waste, and the study adds a small example of low-cost dashboard design in food retail.
Pathway. Business Intelligence and Dashboards

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A design-and-test study that builds a prototype and tests it with users.
Data. Twelve months of daily unsold-bread counts from the chain's own sales system, shared under a written agreement dated 2 October 2026.
Method. Interviews to select the indicators (objective 1), a dashboard built in a free business intelligence tool (objective 2) and a short usability questionnaire (objective 3).
Evaluation. At least five of the six managers should complete three set tasks in under two minutes each, and the average score on a ten-item usability scale should reach 70 out of 100.
Feasibility. The main risk is that managers have little time for testing, so I will schedule each session for 20 minutes during quiet hours.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Indicator interviews and prototype build: December 2026 to January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Usability tests and write-up: March to April 2027
M4 Final submission: 14 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Adler (2019) describes dashboards for retail. Bianchi (2020) reviews waste metrics in food service. Costa (2021) lists common dashboard design errors.

References
Adler, A. (2019) Dashboards for retail managers. Journal of Applied Analytics, 12(3).
